items.title: Burrill Crohn interviewed by Monk Rowe, Woodstock, New York, January 3, 2012
items.q: You have the vibrato of the clarinetist and then you have Sidney Bechet, which brought vibrato to a whole other level. He made vibrato an art form.

ctx.x: In that film, and in other places, when I read about jazz, I sometimes object to the idea that changes in music, jazz especially, are often because of social issues. To me they leave out the thing about people just experiment because they can, and because it feels good to do something new, or — Evan Christopher, who’s a clarinetist we’ve had at the college, had this interesting theory about why vibrato with the early New Orleans clarinetists, and it had to do with playing with out of tune pianos. You know, that…
Wait a minute. There’s vibrato and there’s vibrato. You have the vibrato of the clarinetist and then you have Sidney Bechet, which brought vibrato to a whole other level. He made vibrato an art form.
